To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) predation risk varies with position in the colonial web, (2) foraging success also varies with position, (3) the relationship between predation risk, foraging success and position is different for different age (size) classes, (4) this results in ontogenetic shifts within colonies as spiders move into the colony core as they mature.
the costs of living in a colony are greater for small and large individuals, but the benefits of colony living are higher for small individuals.

the risk of predation and foraging success vary with position in a colony of the colonial web building spider Metepeira incrassat a, that larger spiders are more aggressive than smaller spiders and that this aggression is directed towards smaller spiders in the colony, that smaller spiders are more vulnerable than larger spiders to attack by predators, and that larger spiders have a higher rate of prey capture than smaller spiders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of colonial behavior in spiders.
the ontogenetic changes in behavior that are associated with changes in size and age in a colony forming spider.
the evolution of sociality, and how the costs and benefits of group living may change over an animal's life cycle, resulting in ontogenetic changes in behavior and social organization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the spatial variation in fitness tradeoffs associated with age (size) and position in the colony is the result of a dynamic balance of predation risk and food availability, with the risk of predation decreasing with age.
the selfish herd effect is a dynamic phenomenon in which the costs and benefits of social aggregation shift as spiders mature.
the ontogeny of a spider colony is a result of trade-offs in foraging success and predation risk that are influenced by size and position within the colony.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the selfish herd effect is not just about avoiding predation, but about foraging success as well.
the colony structure ofM. incrassata is a compromise between the conflicting demands for foraging success and predator avoidance.
the selfish herd effect is a consequence of the ontogenetic shift in the trade off between foraging success and predation risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ontogenetic shifts within a colony are driven by the interaction of age (size) related fitness tradeoffs between risk and foraging.
the spatial position within a colony is a function of the age of the spider.
the selfish herd effect is not static, and that ontogenetic shifts within colonies may be a key component of the evolution of colony structure in social spiders.
